1F (Number Theory)

Words: 106 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 106
1F OurBigBook.com
The Prime number theorem says π(x)∼x/logx as x→∞. Bertrand's postulate says that for every integer n≥2 there is a prime number strictly between n and 2n.
To count S-smooth numbers, split each prime exponent into its parity and an even part. This gives the unique expression n=ab2, where a is a squarefree product of a subset of S. There are 2∣S∣ possible a, while b≤x​ whenever n≤x. The squarefree-part bound for smooth numbers therefore gives fS​(x)≤2∣S∣⌊x​⌋≤2∣S∣x​.
For an integer x≥1, take S to be all prime numbers at most x. Every positive integer at most x is then S-smooth, so x≤2π(x)x​. Taking logarithms yields
π(x)≥2log2logx​.​
(1)

The cosine addition identities give the same recurrence for cos(nt), so mathematical induction proves Tn​(cost)=cos(nt). For n≥1, the leading coefficient is 2n−1, proving that its polynomial degree is exactly n.

False. A function of cost is even in t, whereas sin(nt) is odd. If the identity held, replacing t by −t would imply sin(nt)=0 for every t, contradicted by t=π/(2n). Thus no polynomial of any degree has the required property.

3G (Geometry of Group Actions)

Words: 145 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 145
3G OurBigBook.com
Put the cube's vertices at (±1,±1,±1). Squared distances between distinct vertices are 4,8,12 according as one, two or three coordinates differ. Four mutually equidistant vertices cannot all differ in one coordinate, since the cube has no triangles, or in three coordinates, since each vertex has only one antipode. They must differ in two coordinates. The two regular tetrahedra are therefore precisely the sets xyz=1 and xyz=−1.
The full symmetry group G consists of signed coordinate permutations, so ∣G∣=23⋅3!=48. These maps permute the two tetrahedra. The stabilizer H of the first has order 24 and acts faithfully on its four vertices: a linear map fixing the tetrahedron fixes a spanning set. Thus H≅S4​. Central inversion −I swaps the tetrahedra and commutes with every element of H, giving the direct-product decomposition of the cube symmetry group
G≅S4​×C2​.​
(2)
Here H preserves one tetrahedron; it is not the subgroup consisting only of rotations.

4G (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 74 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 74
4G OurBigBook.com
A uniquely decodable code is a map whose extension by concatenation to finite strings is injective. Write ℓj​ for its codeword lengths and assume the target alphabet has size a≥2. The Kraft–McMillan inequality gives K=∑j​a−ℓj​≤1. The Gibbs inequality says D(p∥q)=∑j​pj​log(pj​/qj​)≥0 for probability distributions p,q, with the usual convention for zero probabilities.
Set qj​=a−ℓj​/K. For Shannon entropy H(p)=−∑j​pj​logpj​, the Gibbs inequality becomes
0≤−H(p)+(loga)∑j​pj​ℓj​+logK.
(3)
Since logK≤0, the entropy lower bound for prefix codes also applies to this uniquely decodable code:
Eℓ≥logaH(p)−logK​≥logaH(p)​.​
(4)

5I (Statistical Modelling)

Words: 184 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 184
5I OurBigBook.com
The command fits independent grouped binomial distributions Yj​∼Bin(Nj​,pj​), using the supplied totals as trial counts. The logistic regression has the additive linear predictor
η​=−3.06073−1.270791{Kid}​−0.372111{M}​,p​=1+eη​eη​​.​
(5)
The reference category is adult females. The age and gender coefficients are conditional log odds ratios: the fitted odds for a child are multiplied by e−1.27079≈0.281, and those for a male by e−0.37211≈0.689.
The coefficients are maximum-likelihood estimates, found by Newton's method or iteratively reweighted least squares. With design matrix X and Wjj​=Nj​p​j​(1−p​j​), the estimated covariance matrix is (XTWX)−1; the printed standard errors are square roots of its diagonal entries. Each Wald test compares a coefficient with zero using its estimate divided by its standard error, approximately a standard normal distribution under the null. The age and gender effects are strongly significant. The intercept test instead tests whether the reference probability is 1/2.
The fitted probabilities are about 0.04476 for adult females, 0.03128 for adult males, 0.01298 for female children, and 0.008981 for male children. Adult females have the largest fitted probability, about 4.48%. The residual deviance is 0.06514 on 4−3=1 degree of freedom; comparison with a chi-squared distribution gives p≈0.799. There is no evidence here that an age–gender interaction is needed, under the assumed independent binomial distribution model.

6B (Mathematical Biology)

Words: 104 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 104
6B OurBigBook.com
Let D=Q/V0​ be the dilution rate. Population loss is DN, and nutrient loss by consumption is NK(C)/V0​, so mass conservation gives
N˙=γNK(C)−DN,C˙=D(C0​−C)−V0​NK(C)​.
(6)
Use the dimensionless variables τ=Dt, c=C/K0​, and n=NKmax​/(QK0​). Substitution into the Monod equation gives the stated system with
α=QγKmax​V0​​,β=K0​C0​​.​
(7)
For a positive equilibrium, the first equation requires αc/(1+c)=1. Hence c∗​=1/(α−1) and n∗​=α(β−c∗​), both positive exactly under the specified inequalities.
Writing A=αn∗​/(1+c∗​)2>0, the Jacobian matrix at this equilibrium is
J=(0−1/α​A−1−A/α​),specJ={−1,−A/α}.​
(8)
Both eigenvalues are negative, so the state is locally asymptotically stable. The Monod chemostat equilibrium and relaxation also makes one decay rate transparent: z=c+n/α satisfies z′=β−z, independently of the uptake kinetics.

7E (Dynamical Systems)

Words: 109 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 109
7E OurBigBook.com
Introduce the vector x=(t,y,y′,…,y(k−1))∈Rk+1. Its autonomous ordinary differential equation is
x˙=(1,x2​,x3​,…,xk​,g(x0​,x1​,…,xk​)),
(9)
where the coordinate indices start at zero. Appending the clock removes the explicit time dependence.
For a vector field with local existence and uniqueness, its flow ϕt​(x) is the solution at elapsed time t starting at x. The uniqueness theorem for ordinary differential equations gives ϕs​(ϕt​(x))=ϕs+t​(x) whenever both sides are defined. The orbit is O(x)={ϕt​(x):t lies in its maximal interval}. For a forward-complete solution its omega-limit set is
ω(x)=⋂T≥0​{ϕt​(x):t≥T}​,
(10)
equivalently the set of limits along sequences tn​→∞. A homoclinic orbit is a nonconstant complete orbit approaching the same equilibrium as t→−∞ and t→∞. This last definition concerns a general autonomous system; the appended clock itself cannot approach an equilibrium.

Words: 93 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 93
8B OurBigBook.com
Continuation around one positively oriented loop induces an invertible linear map M on the two-dimensional solution space. Its inverse is continuation around the reversed loop. Over C, choose an eigenvector with eigenvalue λ=0, and let w be the corresponding nonzero solution. After continuation it becomes λw.
Choose σ with e2πiσ=λ. The product h(z)=z−σw(z) has trivial monodromy, so it is single-valued and holomorphic on the punctured disc. Its Laurent series, convergent on compact subannuli, gives the Monodromy eigenfunction Laurent representation
w(z)=zσn=−∞∑∞​cn​zn.​
(11)
No assumption of a regular singular point has been made, so the negative part need not terminate.

9C OurBigBook.com
For variations qi​+εηi​ with ηi​(t1​)=ηi​(t2​)=0, differentiation of the action and integration by parts give
δS=∫t1​t2​​(Lqi​​−dtd​Lq˙​i​​)ηi​dt.
(12)
The fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations therefore yields the Euler-Lagrange equations dLq˙​i​​/dt=Lqi​​. An ignorable coordinate has Lqj​​=0, so its conjugate momentum pj​=Lq˙​j​​ is constant.
For the sphere, φ is ignorable and
pφ​=ma2sin2θφ˙​,H=2ma2​(θ˙2+sin2θφ˙​2)+V(θ).​
(13)
The Hamiltonian is the mechanical energy. Along solutions, H˙=−∂L/∂t=0, because the Lagrangian has no explicit time dependence.

10A (Cosmology)

Words: 99 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 99
10A OurBigBook.com
In a spatially flat FLRW metric, a radial null geodesic satisfies dχ/dt=±c/a(t). For a source and observer at fixed comoving separation, χ=∫te​t0​​cdt/a(t). Applying this to successive wave crests gives dt0​/a(t0​)=dte​/a(te​) and therefore the cosmological redshift 1+z=a(t0​)/a(te​).
Each photon's energy is reduced by 1+z, and the arrival interval is increased by 1+z. The received power crossing the observation sphere is consequently L/(1+z)2. Its physical area is 4πa(t0​)2∣x∣2, so the radiative flux is
F=4πa(t0​)2∣x∣2(1+z)2L​.​
(14)
This is the luminosity distance relation with dL​=(1+z)a(t0​)∣x∣. The Euclidean area formula presumes spatial flatness; in a curved FLRW metric the transverse comoving distance replaces ∣x∣.

11G (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 184 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 184
11G OurBigBook.com
For binary linear codes of length n, the bar product of binary linear codes is C1​∣C2​={(u,u+v):u∈C1​,v∈C2​}. The parametrization is injective and linear, so its dimension is k1​+k2​. If v=0, a nonzero word has Hamming weight at least 2d1​; if v=0, wt(u)+wt(u+v)≥wt(v)≥d2​. Taking (u,u) and (0,v) of minimum weight shows
dim(C1​∣C2​)=k1​+k2​,d(C1​∣C2​)=min(2d1​,d2​).​
(15)
For a∈C2⊥​,b∈C1⊥​, the inner product of (u,u+v) and (a,a+b) is u⋅b+v⋅a+v⋅b=0, since C2​⊆C1​. The spaces have complementary dimensions, proving (C1​∣C2​)⊥=C2⊥​∣C1⊥​.
Define the Reed-Muller code RM(d,r) by evaluating all multilinear polynomials of total degree at most r at the 2d points of F2d​. The squarefree monomials are independent functions, giving dimension ∑j=0r​(jd​). Splitting according to the last variable gives the Reed-Muller bar-product recursion RM(d,r)=RM(d−1,r)∣RM(d−1,r−1), with the endpoint codes interpreted in the usual way. The distance recursion gives 2d−r.
To identify the Dual of a Reed-Muller code, multiply a monomial of degree at most r by one of degree at most d−r−1. The product omits some variable, so its sum over F2d​ is even and its binary inner product is zero. The binomial dimension identity then gives
RM(d,r)⊥=RM(d,d−r−1)(0≤r<d).​
(16)

Using the diameter normalization, define Hδd​(E)=inf{∑j​(diamUj​)d:E⊆⋃j​Uj​, diamUj​≤δ} and the Hausdorff measure Hd(E)=limδ↓0​Hδd​(E). The Hausdorff dimension is inf{d:Hd(E)=0}, equivalently sup{d:Hd(E)=∞}.
The Cantor set is the intersection of the sets left by successively removing open middle thirds from [0,1]. At level k it has 2k Cantor cylinders of diameter 3−k. For s=log2/log3, their total s-cost is 2k3−ks=1, so Hs(C)≤1.
The random series ξ=∑n≥1​Xn​3−n converges absolutely, and its ternary digits are all zero or two. Thus ξ∈C and its law is the Cantor Bernoulli measure. Each level-k cylinder has probability 2−k. Distinct such intervals have separation at least 3−k; a set U of smaller diameter meets at most one. If 3−(k+1)≤diamU<3−k, then
P(ξ∈U)≤2−k=2(3−(k+1))s≤2(diamU)s.
(17)
Sets of diameter zero have probability zero, since the measure has no measure atoms; diameters at least one give the bound trivially. For arbitrary nonmeasurable sets use outer probability. Any countable cover of C therefore satisfies 1≤∑j​P∗(ξ∈Uj​)≤2∑j​(diamUj​)s. Hence
21​≤Hs(C)≤1,dimH​C=log3log2​.​
(18)
The last implication follows by multiplying the s-costs by powers of the cover diameter: measures above s vanish and those below s are infinite.

13I OurBigBook.com
The first command fits independent Poisson random variables with means μj​ and a log link. For concentration x and strain indicator s, its fitted linear predictor is
logμ​=4.14443−1.47253x+0.33667s−0.12534xs.
(19)
The interaction allows different concentration slopes in the two strains. At x=0 the second strain's mean is multiplied by e0.33667; its slope is −1.47253−0.12534. These are multiplicative changes in counts, not changes in probabilities.
The maximum-likelihood estimates use the Poisson regression likelihood. With design matrix X, estimated information XTdiag(μ​j​)X gives the inverse covariance matrix; diagonal square roots give the standard errors. The printed Wald tests use approximately standard-normal coefficient-to-error ratios. Fuel and strain effects are strong, whereas the interaction has p=0.182, suggesting a common slope.
H2​ removes just the interaction; H3​ also removes strain. Their parameter counts are four, three and two. Under the usual large-sample likelihood-ratio test, D2​−D1​=1.78089 is compared with χ12​ and is below 3.841459, so the interaction is not required at 5%. By contrast, D3​−D2​=32.61857 is far above that threshold, so the strain main effect should remain. Comparing H3​ directly with H1​ uses D3​−D1​ and two degrees of freedom.
For an approximate absolute goodness-of-fit test, compare D1​=84.59557 with χ70−42​; its upper-tail probability is about 0.061. For H2​, D2​=86.37646 on 67 degrees of freedom has p≈0.056. The additive model H2​ is the preferred parsimonious fit at 5%, subject to the independent Poisson distribution and large-sample assumptions. The printed nine rows are only a subset; the supplied fitted output refers to all 70 observations.

J is entire in z. Along the fixed Pochhammer contour, the continued logarithms of t and 1−t are bounded, and the contour stays away from both branch points. The integrand exp((z−1)logt+(b−1)log(1−t)) is entire in z with uniform bounds on each compact parameter set. Differentiation under the contour integral is therefore valid to every order.

ii

Words: 60 Articles: 1
14B OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 60
ii OurBigBook.com
Contract the loops in the Pochhammer contour onto the interval (0,1). When Rez,Reb>0, the small-circle contributions tend to zero. The two clockwise circuits change the branches by e−2πib and e−2πiz, and the return circuits undo them. The four interval contributions sum to
J(z)=(1−e−2πiz)(1−e−2πib)∫01​tz−1(1−t)b−1dt.
(20)
Using the Beta function and 1−e−2πiu=2ie−πiusin(πu) gives
J(z)=−4e−πi(z+b)sin(πz)sin(πb)B(z,b).​
(21)

iii

Words: 90 Articles: 1
14B OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 90
iii OurBigBook.com
Because b is not an integer, the coefficient sin(πb) is nonzero. The expression of B in terms of the entire function J can therefore have poles only at integral z, and at most simple ones. Positive integers are removable: B(z,b) is already analytic there for Reb>0, and analytic continuation in b gives
B(n,b)=b(b+1)⋯(b+n−1)(n−1)!​(n≥1).
(22)
Thus J vanishes at those integers, cancelling the denominator zero. The Gamma function formula B(z,b)=Γ(z)Γ(b)/Γ(z+b) identifies the remaining singularities:
z=−m (m=0,1,…),Resz=−m​B(z,b)=m!Γ(b−m)(−1)mΓ(b)​.​
(23)
For nonintegral b, these residues are nonzero, so every listed singularity is a genuine simple pole.

Solution

Words: 170
15A OurBigBook.com
Differentiate the Friedmann equation and use the cosmological continuity equation to obtain H˙+H2=−(4πG/3)(ρ+3P/c2). The relation extends to turning points by continuity. Radiation obeys ρR​=ρR0​a−4, while dark energy with PΛ​=−ρΛ​c2 has constant density. Substitution at a(t0​)=1 gives kc2=βH02​, and at arbitrary a gives
H2=H02​a4a4−βa2+β​,H˙=−βH02​a42−a2​.
(24)
Put x=a2. For β>4, the upward-opening polynomial P(x)=x2−βx+β has roots x±​=(β±β(β−4)​)/2, with 1<x−​<2<x+​. The expanding Big Bang branch reaches x−​ in finite time. There H=0 but H˙<0, so expansion turns to contraction; it returns to a=0 in finite time, a Big Crunch. A sketch of a4H2/H02​=P(x) has the forbidden negative interval between the roots, while a4H˙/H02​=β(x−2) is a line crossing zero at two.
For β=4, P(x)=(x−2)2. The branch starting at zero has x˙=2H0​(2−x), giving
a(t)=2(1−e−2H0​t)​.​
(25)
At small t, a∼2H0​t​, the radiation-dominated scale factor. At large t, a=2​[1−21​e−2H0​t+O(e−4H0​t)]. It approaches an Einstein static universe with equal radiation and dark-energy densities, rather than recollapsing or entering unbounded expansion.

16G (Set Theory and Logic)

Words: 317 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 317
16G OurBigBook.com
A complete lattice has every join, hence every directed and finite join. Conversely, if a partially ordered set is directed-complete and has finite joins including the empty join, then for any subset A the set of joins of its finite subsets is nonempty and directed. Its least upper bound is ⋁A. Including the empty join supplies a bottom element and handles A=∅.
For a directed set of partial functions from A to B, their union is a function: any two functions have a common extension, so they agree wherever their domains overlap. This union is exactly their least upper bound in the extension order, proving directed completeness.
Write Cx​ for the intersection of all sets containing x and closed under f and directed joins. Then xRy means y∈Cx​. Reflexivity is immediate, and transitivity follows because any closed set containing x must contain y and then every z with yRz. The upper set [x,∞) is closed: f is inflationary, and a directed join of elements above x is above x. Thus xRy implies x≤y, proving antisymmetry.
If h,k∈H, then xRk(x)Rh(k(x)), so h∘k∈H. Moreover h(k(x))≥h(x) by monotonicity, and h(k(x))≥k(x) by inflationarity. This proves that Hx is directed. Define h0​(x)=⋁Hx. Pointwise monotonicity of every h implies monotonicity of h0​. Since Hx⊆Cx​ and Cx​ is closed under directed joins, xRh0​(x); hence h0​∈H.
The original map f belongs to H by the definition of closedness, so f∘h0​∈H and f(h0​(x))≤h0​(x) by the definition of the join. Inflationarity gives the reverse inequality. Finally, if p=f(p) and p≥x, the lower set (−∞,p] is closed by monotonicity of f and the join property. Thus every h(x) is at most p, and so is h0​(x). This proves the least fixed point from a directed family of maps: h0​(x) is the least fixed point above x.

17H (Graph Theory)

Words: 275 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 275
17H OurBigBook.com
Label four face colors by F22​. Give each edge the sum of its two adjacent face labels. This is nonzero because adjacent faces differ. At a cubic vertex the three face labels are pairwise distinct, so their three edge sums are the three different nonzero elements. This is a Tait coloring.
Conversely, label the three edge colors by the nonzero elements of F22​, whose sum is zero. Choose a base face with label zero and label any other face by summing crossed edge labels along a path in the dual graph. The result is independent of the path: a simple closed dual path encloses vertices, and summing the zero incident sums at these vertices leaves exactly its crossed boundary edges, since interior edges occur twice. General closed paths decompose into such cycles. Adjacent labels differ by a nonzero edge label, giving a four-color face coloring. The assumption that every edge borders distinct faces excludes bridges in a graph and ensures this map coloring is the relevant one.
The equivalence fails on a torus. Use the Heawood torus map. On seven vertices indexed modulo seven, take the triangles Ai​=(i,i+1,i+3) and Bi​=(i,i+3,i+2). Each edge of K7​ occurs in exactly two oppositely oriented triangles; each vertex link is a six-cycle, for example 1,3,2,6,4,5,1 at zero. This is a connected closed orientable surface with Euler characteristic 7−21+14=0, hence a torus.
Its dual graph is cubic, with Ai​ adjacent to Bi​,Bi+1​,Bi−2​. The three offsets partition its edges into perfect matchings, giving a Tait coloring. Its seven faces are discs and their adjacency graph is K7​, so they need seven colors. The obstruction to the planar proof is a possible nonzero edge-label sum around a noncontractible cycle.

The continuous dual space X∗ consists of bounded linear functionals with operator norm ∥v∥=sup∥x∥≤1​∣v(x)∣. For an operator-norm Cauchy sequence (vn​), each (vn​(x)) is Cauchy in R. Define v(x)=limn​vn​(x). It is linear, and bounded because the Cauchy sequence has uniformly bounded norms. Passing to the pointwise limit in ∣(vn​−vm​)(x)∣≤ε∥x∥ gives ∥vn​−v∥≤ε. Thus X∗ is a Banach space, even when X is incomplete.
The canonical map ϕ(x)(v)=v(x) is linear and satisfies ∥ϕ(x)∥≤∥x∥. For x=0, the norm-one functional tx↦t∥x∥ on its span extends by the Hahn-Banach theorem to a norm-one functional on X. Hence ∥ϕ(x)∥≥∥x∥, proving that ϕ is an isometry and therefore injective.
For a nonsurjective example take X=c0​ with the supremum norm. It is complete as a closed subspace of ℓ∞. Every functional is given by an ℓ1 sequence: finite-coordinate sign tests give summability of its coefficients, and truncation of each c0​ vector gives the series representation. Conversely any ℓ1 sequence defines such a bounded functional. Similarly (ℓ1)∗=ℓ∞, so c0∗∗​=ℓ∞. The canonical image is the null sequences; the constant sequence one is outside it. Thus c0​ is a nonreflexive Banach space.

Use stereographic projection charts φ(X,Y,Z)=(X+iY)/(1−Z) away from the north pole and ψ(X,Y,Z)=(X−iY)/(1+Z) away from the south pole. On their overlap ψ=1/φ, a holomorphic transition function, defining the Riemann sphere.
Where F avoids the north pole, φ∘F is an ordinary holomorphic function exactly when F is holomorphic. Near a north-pole value, the other chart gives ψ∘F=1/(φ∘F); a zero of this holomorphic coordinate becomes a pole of φ∘F. This proves the correspondence with meromorphic functions. On a disconnected domain one must also allow components mapped constantly to infinity, or state the correspondence on each nonconstant component. Applying the same reciprocal charts at source and target infinity shows that every nonconstant rational function defines a holomorphic sphere map.
The multiplicity of the value a at infinity is the zero order at w=0 of f(1/w)−a when a is finite, and of 1/f(1/w) when a=∞. For coprime polynomials P,Q, the degree of a rational map of the Riemann sphere is n=max(degP,degQ), also its total number of poles with multiplicities.
The quotient rule f′=(P′Q−PQ′)/Q2 gives the upper bound degf′≤2n. Each finite pole of order m contributes order m+1 to f′. If degP>degQ, infinity contributes an additional order degP−degQ−1 when this is positive. Counting gives the degree bounds for the derivative of a rational function

The lower bound is attained by f=zn; the upper by f=1/(zn−1), whose n simple finite poles become double poles. Product degrees are not additive: f=z and g=(z+1)/z both have degree one, but fg=z+1 also has degree one because the zero and pole cancel.

E1​ is a Dynkin system but not a pi-system. The whole ten-point set has even cardinality, complements preserve parity, and disjoint unions of even sets are even. Two even sets can intersect in a singleton, for example {1,2} and {2,3}.
E2​ is neither. The infinite set N∖{1} belongs to it, but its singleton complement does not, so it is not a Dynkin system. The two infinite sets {1}∪{2,4,6,…} and {1,3,5,…} intersect in the excluded singleton, so it is not a pi-system.
E3​ is a pi-system but not a Dynkin system. Intersections of bounded open intervals are bounded open intervals or empty. However, the family does not contain the whole underlying set R. None of the three families is a sigma-algebra.

The uniqueness theorem for measures says that two measures agreeing on a generating pi-system agree on its generated sigma-algebra, provided they are finite with the same total mass, or there is a common increasing exhaustion by pi-system sets of finite measure.
For the finite case let D={A:μ(A)=ν(A)}. Equality of total masses gives closure under complements, and countable additivity gives closure under disjoint countable unions. Thus D is a Dynkin system containing the generating pi-system. The pi-lambda theorem puts the entire generated sigma-algebra inside D.
For the exhaustion version, let En​↑E with En​ in the pi-system and μ(En​)=ν(En​)<∞. The finite measures A↦μ(A∩En​) and A↦ν(A∩En​) agree on the generating pi-system, since it is intersection-closed. The finite proof applies, and continuity from below of a measure as n→∞ gives μ(A)=ν(A) for every measurable A. A finiteness hypothesis is essential to this standard extension-uniqueness statement.

A sufficient statistic has a conditional law of X given T independent of the parameter. An ordinary ancillary statistic has a distribution independent of the whole parameter. A partial ancillary statistic for ψ has a law free of ψ, though it may depend on the nuisance parameter λ. The conditionality principle uses the conditional experiment given the observed value of S; removing λ additionally requires the conditional law of C given S to be free of it.
The factorization requested in the PDF expresses this stronger ancillary conditioning that eliminates a nuisance parameter. There is also a normalization typo: the conditional factor must satisfy ∑c​ϕC​(c,s;ψ)=1 for each fixed s, rather than the printed double sum over s and c.
Under that nuisance-eliminating interpretation, take ϕ0​(x) to be the parameter-free conditional probability of X=x given (C,S), ϕC​(c,s;ψ) to be the conditional probability of C=c given S=s, and ϕS​(s;λ) the marginal probability of S=s. The conditional probability rule gives f=ϕ0​ϕC​ϕS​, with the three separate normalizations. Conversely summing over the fibers first gives the joint law ϕC​ϕS​, then summing over c gives ϕS​ and dividing gives the required conditional law ϕC​. The factorization also proves sufficiency of (C,S).
This equivalence is not valid for ordinary ancillarity alone: a constant S is always ancillary, and T=X is sufficient, but conditioning on a constant generally leaves the nuisance parameter present. Thus the distinction matters to the conclusion.
For the independent gamma distributed sample, the joint log-likelihood is
ℓ(a,b)=nalogb−nlogΓ(a)+(a−1)∑j​logxj​−b∑j​xj​.

The proposed factorization would write this as a data-only term plus a function of a and data plus a function of b and data. It would therefore force its mixed derivative to vanish. In fact
∂a∂b∂2ℓ​=bn​=0.​
(40)
The mixed log-likelihood derivative obstruction to parameter separation rules out this exact nuisance-eliminating factorization. It does not rule out ordinary ancillary statistics: a constant statistic still qualifies, and (∑logXj​,∑Xj​) is sufficient for the full two-parameter family.

ψ​(p)=2πℏ​1​∫R​e−ipx/ℏψ(x)dx,ψ(x)=2πℏ​1​∫R​eipx/ℏψ​(p)dp.

The kinetic term is multiplication by p2/(2m), and the potential has momentum kernel ⟨p∣V∣p′⟩=(2πℏ)−1∫V(x)e−i(p−p′)x/ℏdx. Thus the Schrödinger equation becomes
(2mp2​−E)ψ​(p)=−2πℏ1​∫R2​V(x)e−i(p−p′)x/ℏψ​(p′)dxdp′.
(54)
For the attractive delta potential, V(x)=−(ℏ2λ/m)δ(x), the kernel is the constant −ℏλ/(2πm), giving the stated positive right-hand side. For ψ​=N/(p2+α2) with α>0, constancy of the left side requires E=−α2/(2m). Since ∫dp/(p2+α2)=π/α, its coefficient equation gives
α=ℏλ,E=−2mℏ2λ2​.​
(55)
Finally, transforming λ​e−λ∣x∣ gives ψ​=2λ3/2ℏ2/[2πℏ​(p2+ℏ2λ2)], verifying the same momentum-space form and energy.

33A (Applications of Quantum Mechanics)

Words: 212 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 212
33A OurBigBook.com
The incoming and outgoing coefficients give the scattering matrix
S(k)=g(−k)g(k)​=(k−iκ)(k−iα)(k+iκ)(k+iα)​.​
(56)
It obeys S(−k)=S(k)−1 and S(k∗)∗=S(k)−1, so ∣S(k)∣=1 for real k, as required by elastic unitarity. With S=e2iδ, the scattering phase shift satisfies tanδ=k(κ+α)/(k2−κα). The inverse tangent needs a continuous branch: taking δ(∞)=0 gives δ(0)=π. Equivalently δ=arctan(κ/k)+arctan(α/k) for k>0.
The scattering length follows from kcotδ=−1/as​+O(k2):
as​=κακ+α​.​
(57)
For a putative bound state put k=iη, η>0. The incoming term grows as eηr, so its coefficient must vanish. The incoming Jost function is F(k)=g(−k)=(k−iκ)/(k+iα); its only upper-half-plane zero is iκ. Under the regular-potential assumption this gives one bound state, with E=−ℏ2κ2/(2m).​ The pole at iα in S instead comes from the outgoing numerator: it is a redundant pole of a scattering matrix, not a second normalizable state. The S-matrix alone, without its incoming/outgoing analytic structure, would tempt an incorrect count of two states.
For completeness, the nonsingular Eckart realization of this Jost function requires α>κ, as discussed in dipot.ulb.ac.be/dspace/bitstream/2013/373712/4/2306.12216.pdf. The supplied positive constants alone do not establish such a realization in every ordering; a coincident pole is likewise not evidence for two states.
There is no positive-energy scattering resonance. Indeed δ′(k)=−κ/(k2+κ2)−α/(k2+α2)<0, and the s-wave total partial-wave total scattering cross-section is 4π(κ+α)2/[(k2+κ2)(k2+α2)], strictly decreasing for k>0. All poles are on the imaginary axis, with no oscillatory decaying resonance pole.

34E (Electrodynamics)

Words: 136 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 136
34E OurBigBook.com
Assume an infinite, stationary, uniform thin wire, and no added external homogeneous fields. Its four-current is jμ=(σ,0,0,J)δ(x)δ(y). A boost along the wire leaves the transverse delta functions unchanged and transforms the time and longitudinal components, giving
σ′=γ(σ−vJ),J′=γ(J−vσ).​
(58)
The densities are measured per unit simultaneous length in their respective frames; treating charge alone as invariant per unchanged coordinate length would miss the current contribution.
For a coaxial cylinder, Gauss's law gives Er​(2πrL)=μ0​σL in the stated c=1 units. For a circular loop, Ampère's law gives Bφ​2πr=μ0​J. Thus Er​=μ0​σ/(2πr) and Bφ​=μ0​J/(2πr). The same reasoning in the primed frame gives the same expressions with primed densities.
Since z×φ​=−r and z×r=φ​, the Lorentz transformation of electromagnetic fields gives Er′​=γ(Er​−vBφ​) and Bφ′​=γ(Bφ​−vEr​). Substituting the laboratory fields reproduces the primed-density formulas exactly; parallel components vanish in both frames.

35A (General Relativity)

Words: 131 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 131
35A OurBigBook.com
With the stated curvature convention, the Ricci tensor is Rbd​=Rabad​ and the scalar curvature is R=gbdRbd​. Contract the differential Bianchi identity once to give the divergence of the Riemann tensor, then again with the inverse metric. The curvature antisymmetries yield ∇aRab​−∇b​R+∇aRab​=0, so ∇aRab​=21​∇b​R.
The Einstein field equations are Gab​+Λgab​=(8πG/c4)Tab​, with Gab​=Rab​−21​Rgab​. The contracted Bianchi identity makes the left side divergence-free, enforcing the local stress-energy conservation law ∇aTab​=0 and ensuring consistency of the matter equations with the gravitational constraints.
For a scalar, second covariant derivatives commute. Commuting a further derivative past the resulting covector introduces Ricci curvature, giving ∇2∇a​ϕ=∇a​∇2ϕ+Rab​∇bϕ.
Now Rab​=∇a​∇b​ϕ implies R=∇2ϕ. Taking its divergence and using that commutation formula gives 21​∇b​R=∇b​R+Rba​∇aϕ, hence ∇b​R=−2Rba​∇aϕ. Meanwhile ∇b​(∇a​ϕ∇aϕ)=2Rba​∇aϕ. Adding proves
R+∇a​ϕ∇aϕ=constant on each connected component.​
(59)
In Riemannian signature this is the steady gradient Ricci soliton scalar identity, with soliton potential f=−ϕ.

36B (Fluid Dynamics II)

Words: 212 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 212
36B OurBigBook.com
For lubrication theory, take layer thickness H, horizontal length L and speed U. Require aspect ratio ε=H/L≪1, small surface slopes, inertial ratio UH2/(νL)≪1, and slow evolution H2/(νT)≪1. The longitudinal viscous term then dominates the longitudinal derivative term, while transverse momentum is hydrostatic.
Here ε∼α and U∼gH2α/ν, so sufficient conditions are α≪1 and gH3α2/ν2≪1, together with the slow-time condition. With atmospheric pressure at the surface, p=patm​+ρgcosα(h−y). No slip at the wall and zero surface shear give
u=νg​(sinα−cosαhx​)(hy−y2/2),q=3νgh3​(sinα−cosαhx​).
(60)
Depth-integrated mass conservation, ht​+qx​=0, therefore gives the stated equation with
A=3νgsinα​∼3νgα​,B=3νgcosα​∼3νg​.​
(61)
A steady linear profile with hx​=A/B=tanα has zero flux: its free surface is horizontal in laboratory coordinates, so the hydrostatic gradient balances downslope gravity. A constant-depth profile also gives steady through-flow.
For the travelling front of a gravity-driven thin film, set h=F(ξ), ξ=x−ct. Integrating and using the dry tip gives −cF=−AF3+BF3F′. The state F→h0​, F′→0 behind the front fixes c=Ah02​​. Consequently F′=(A/B)(1−h02​/F2), and integration with F(0)=0 yields
ξ=AB​[F+2h0​​logh0​+Fh0​−F​].​
(62)
This tends to −∞ as F↑h0​. Expanding at zero gives ξ∼−BF3/(3Ah02​), so F∼(−3cξ/B)1/3.​ The divergent slope at the formal tip violates the small-slope approximation sufficiently close to the contact line; the interior profile is the lubrication result.

37C (Waves)

Words: 126 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 126
37C OurBigBook.com
Take shear-horizontal waves with displacement u=(0,0,w(x,y,t)). This is divergence-free, so the elastic equation reduces to ρwtt​=μ(wxx​+wyy​). Rigid boundaries require w=0 at y=0,h, giving modes w=Asin(nπy/h)cos(kx−ωt), n≥1. With shear speed cs​=μ/ρ​, the dispersion relation is
ω2=cs2​(k2+h2n2π2​),ωc,n​=hnπcs​​.​
(63)
For k>0, the phase velocity is vp​=ω/k>cs​ and the group velocity is vg​=dω/dk=cs2​k/ω<cs​, with vp​vg​=cs2​.
The kinetic energy density is T=ρwt2​/2. The only strains are exz​=wx​/2 and eyz​=wy​/2, together with their symmetric counterparts; thus the isotropic linear-elastic energy density is W=μ(wx2​+wy2​)/2. Average over one temporal period and integrate across the layer. The sine- and cosine-squared transverse integrals are both h/2, giving
⟨∫0h​Tdy⟩=8ρA2ω2h​=8μA2h​(k2+h2n2π2​)=⟨∫0h​Wdy⟩.​
(64)
The guided shear-horizontal mode has average equipartition after both operations; a time average at a fixed transverse point alone need not give equality.

Solution

a OurBigBook.com
Apply the numerical method to the test equation y′=λy and put z=hλ. Its linear stability domain is the set of z for which the computed amplification is stable, for a one-step method ∣R(z)∣≤1 with all stage solves well-defined. The method is A-stable if this includes the whole closed left half-plane (or its interior with boundary limits).

b

Words: 87 Articles: 1
38C OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 87
b OurBigBook.com
The Runge-Kutta method has A=(1/41/4+a​1/4−a1/4​) and b=(1/2,1/2)T. Solving the stage equations for y′=λy gives the stability function
R(z)=1+zbT(I−zA)−11=1−z/2+a2z21+z/2+a2z2​.
(65)
For a=0, the denominator roots have positive real parts: real roots are positive from their positive sum and product, while a complex conjugate pair has real part 1/(4a2)>0. For a=0 its sole root is 2. Thus there are no poles or singular stage systems in the left half-plane.
Writing z=x+iy, direct expansion gives
∣1−z/2+a2z2∣2−∣1+z/2+a2z2∣2=−2x(1+a2∣z∣2)≥0(x≤0).
(66)
This proves the A-stability of a symmetric two-stage implicit Runge-Kutta family:
The method is A-stable for every a∈R.​
(67)
